A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with readable text, figures, tables, and equations. However, both reference separate Supplementary Materials that are neither appended nor embedded. Their sampling details, annotation instructions, and additional analyses cannot be compared; the judgments below concern the supplied material.

before.justification: v1 reports original contribution measurements across four creative domains, length and adaptive-attack experiments, and WildChat analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds human-annotation agreement, temperature experiments, output-only estimation results, and multi-round news refinement.

M1.justification: The original measure I(x;y)/I(y) remains. v2 adds an output-only estimator, phi_hat = 1 + N log(tau)/I(y), replacing unavailable conditional information with a threshold-derived bound. This introduces a substantive procedure requiring neither the original prompt nor its generation history.

E1.justification: The four creative domains and WildChat remain. v2 additionally evaluates contribution estimation without access to human input (Figure 8) and three-round news refinement (Figure 9). These introduce distinct information-availability and interaction scenarios beyond v1's single-round, known-input evaluation.

E2.justification: Neither supplied PDF evaluates competing human-contribution measures; AI detectors appear as related work. GPT-4o is added as a generation model in v2 Figure 6, rather than as a competing measurement method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces human agreement evaluation on 1,000 pairs selected for measured gaps above 0.1, a temperature sweep using 0.3, 0.7, and 0.9, and three-round refinement of 1,000 news examples. It also adds GPT-4o generation. These are new protocols; the original 2,000 entries per domain and default temperature 0.7 remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-judgment agreement and disagreement analysis, temperature sensitivity (Figure 4), and contribution evolution during repeated expansion (Figure 9). The existing length and two adaptive-attack analyses remain, so those checks are not new additions.

E5.justification: Both PDFs report five generations per input and retain Table 1's dispersion summaries and median/quartile/1.5-IQR plotting conventions. No new seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates appear in the supplied material.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports 97.4% human agreement and contribution decreases in 87.12% of round 1–2 cases and 94.37% of round 2–3 cases, alongside GPT-4o and output-only results. Retained distributions also change, including Figure 3 and the adaptive-attack plots, although their qualitative trends persist. These are revised or added outcomes, without an established same-setting accuracy improvement.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's original contribution definition, v2 adds Definition 2 for minimal contribution, a geometric-mean probability plausibility criterion, and derivations bounding conditional information and mutual information (Equations 6–10). This is substantive new mathematical content.

C1.justification: Although the abstract is unchanged, v2's introduction expands the contribution to estimating human contribution from any text without knowing its generation process. v1 explicitly leaves unknown-input evaluation for future work. This substantially broadens the claimed scope.

C2.justification: v2 removes the unknown-input and absent-multi-round limitations, explains the minimal-contribution interpretation and negative estimates, and adds temperature-based mechanism reasoning. It also qualifies applicability to nondiscrete modalities and explicitly separates informational contribution from prompt-engineering effectiveness.

D1.justification: New Experimental Setups and Computational Resources sections disclose exact model identifiers, estimation thresholds 0.65 and 0.7, A100 80GB hardware, and average measurement time of 0.33 seconds per sample. Code and data links remain unchanged. Newly specified checkpoints do not establish that retained experiments changed models.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chiang et al.'s Chatbot Arena as inspiration for pairwise human annotation. The positioning against binary AI-text detection and the existing related-work discussion remain substantially unchanged; other reference edits concern numbering or bibliographic presentation.

P1.justification: v2 locally revises dataset motivation, cross-domain explanations, length-control discussion, and probability explanations, while adding subsection headings and an author affiliation. The abstract and broad Results–Discussion–Methods organization remain intact; most expansion introduces scientific content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds temperature, output-only, and multi-round figures (Figures 4, 8, and 9), expands the generalization display from six to eight panels, changes axes and scaling in retained plots, and redesigns the WildChat case display. These substantially extend and revise the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Human judgments, temperature and multi-round checks, and explicit implementation settings strengthen v1's validation and reproducibility. The gains are qualified: 97.4% agreement concerns metric-selected pairs, while the output-only derivation supplies a threshold-dependent lower bound without establishing an attainable minimum. Thus, the broader estimator does not fully resolve the original attribution limitation, but the added validation and documentation provide a supported overall improvement.
